meta.tagline: Brisket smoke, neon cowboys and jazz-age walls under a big sky

pills: A turning point of JFK history

overview.title: Welcome to Dallas
overview.intro: Dallas likes everything big: the sky is wide, the highways are stacked, the steak portions are serious and the smiles generous. Two Texases live beneath the glass towers — the world-class museums of the Arts District on one side, the mural-covered blues streets of Deep Ellum on the other. At Dealey Plaza one of American history's darkest moments stands frozen; across the bridge, the porch-front shops of Bishop Arts tell of everyday life. 'Howdy' here is not folklore but a real greeting — return it, and doors open.

local_word.definition: The Texas contraction of 'how do you do': the official greeting at any hour. No cowboy hat required — at the register, in the elevator, on the trail, everyone says howdy. The reply is howdy again; add a small nod and you've completed the Texas etiquette.

rules.title: Accept the car, choose your hours wisely
rules.description: The Dallas–Fort Worth Metroplex is a vast highway web: a car (or ride app) is essential, but take the 07:30–09:30 and 16:30–18:30 traffic seriously. The DART train covers the Downtown–Deep Ellum–Fair Park line — plan by neighborhood and never underestimate distances.

rules.title: Wake up early for brisket
rules.description: Texas barbecue has one rule: good brisket runs out. The legendary joints hang the 'sold out' sign toward noon — be in line by 11:00. Order at the counter by the pound: ask for the moist side, with a cold beer alongside.

rules.title: Approach Dealey Plaza with respect, and its museum with a ticket
rules.description: The plaza where JFK was shot is open and free, but the Sixth Floor Museum tells the story: buy the ticket ahead and don't skip the audio guide. Ignore the 'conspiracy tour' sellers on the plaza — the history here is heavy enough on its own.

quick_facts.label: Airport
quick_facts.sub: DFW a mega-hub, DAL close to town

quick_facts.label: Language
quick_facts.sub: The Texas drawl is slow and warm

tip.label: The Dallas philosophy
tip.text: The scale here is big but the warmth is personal: the waiter uses your name, the bartender asks your story. Keep the plan loose and leave room for conversation — Dallas's best tips always come from the local at the next table.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: The Metroplex is a highway empire: the car is the base, DART completes it, and the historic trolley decorates Uptown.

items.title: Arriving from the airports
items.description: From DFW the DART orange line reaches Downtown in an hour — cheap and painless; Love Field is ten minutes from town. If renting a car, DFW's rental center is enormous: budget for the shuttle.

items.title: DART light rail
items.description: One of America's longest light-rail networks: the Downtown, Deep Ellum, Fair Park and Plano lines serve visitors well. Buy tickets on the GoPass app — the carless traveler's best friend.

items.title: The car and highway manners
items.description: The stacked interchanges ('mixmasters') frighten at first sight: trust the navigation and change lanes early. Parking is paid Downtown, easy in most neighborhoods — in Texas, the car is freedom itself.

items.title: The M-Line trolley
items.description: Uptown's restored heritage streetcar runs free along McKinney Avenue: wooden benches, brass bells. Pair it with a Katy Trail walk — Dallas's most graceful transport nostalgia.

items.title: Walking within neighborhoods
items.description: Dallas as a whole can't be walked, but its neighborhoods can: Bishop Arts' shops, Deep Ellum's murals, the Arts District's museum axis. Klyde Warren Park bridges the highway on foot.

callout.label: Katy Trail tip
callout.text: Enter the Katy Trail in the late afternoon: the old rail line crosses Uptown as a green corridor, joggers and golden retrievers for company. Exit onto the trolley down McKinney and end the day on a porch bar — Dallas's most local hour.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: In Dallas the choice is a choice of texture: Downtown's towers, Uptown's porches, Deep Ellum's neon or Bishop Arts' bungalow streets.

local_word.definition: The name of the giant urban region spanning Dallas, Fort Worth and dozens of cities between: a constellation of 8 million. A Dallasite describes distance not in minutes but in highway numbers — '20 minutes up I-35' is a form of address. To understand the Metroplex is to understand Texas scale.

items.name: Downtown
items.description: Reunion Tower, Dealey Plaza and the Arts District within walking distance: a wide range from historic hotels to modern towers. Quieter at night — a practical base for the sight-packed traveler.

items.name: Uptown
items.description: McKinney Avenue's restaurants, the trolley and the Katy Trail: Dallas's walkable, young, polished side. The densest nightlife and dining in the city.

items.name: Deep Ellum
items.description: Mural-covered warehouse streets, live music clubs and craft beer: the creative quarter born from the blues. Loud at night, photogenic by day — the address for atmosphere seekers.

items.name: Bishop Arts District
items.description: Boutique shops, bakeries and taquerías among Oak Cliff's porched bungalows: Dallas's village-scale corner. Ten minutes over the bridge to the center — the calm, characterful side.

items.name: Fort Worth (Sundance Square)
items.description: The Metroplex's other star: Sundance Square's plaza, the cowboy heritage of the Stockyards and world-class museums. Giving it a night or two makes this a two-city trip.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: Dallas's calendar is a bargain with the heat: spring and fall are the golden window, summer is a furnace, and October means the State Fair.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Bluebonnet Spring
items.subtitle: Spring · Wildflower roadsides, porch evenings
items.description: April is Texas's flower month: bluebonnet fields paint the roadsides blue and the Arboretum becomes a blossom festival. The air is mild, the patios open — and it's storm season too: thunder asks your plans to stay flexible.

callout.label: Storm note
callout.text: April–May is severe-storm season in Texas: keep weather alerts on, and move indoors for hail and tornado warnings. Storms usually pass within the hour — flexibility is sufficient insurance.

items.label: Summer
items.name: The Texas Furnace
items.subtitle: Summer · 38°C middays, icy air conditioning
items.description: Summer Dallas is serious heat: noon hits 38°C and life moves to air-conditioned interiors and the evening hours. A hotel pool is summer's gold standard — early morning and post-sunset outdoors, museums and tables between.

callout.label: Midday note
callout.text: An open-air tour at summer noon is punishment: set the Arboretum and Katy Trail before 09:00. The frozen margarita is this season's invention and medicine — order it while noting it was born in Dallas.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: State Fair Season
items.subtitle: Autumn · Fair lights, football Fridays, sweet air
items.description: In late September the State Fair of Texas turns Fair Park into a month-long festival: the Big Tex statue, corny dog aromas and the Ferris wheel. October–November air is made for walking — Dallas's most pleasant weeks.

callout.label: Fair tip
callout.text: Go to the State Fair on a weekday morning: the Fletcher's corny dog queue is short and the Big Tex photo calm. The Art Deco fair buildings are a tour of their own — don't miss the 1936 facades.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Mild and Lit
items.subtitle: Winter · Soft days, sudden cold snaps
items.description: Dallas winter is mostly mild: sunny 15°C days surprise no one. Now and then a polar snap ices the city and life slows — museums, barbecue halls and shopping are the season's natural program.

callout.label: December tip
callout.text: In December the Highland Park lights are a city classic: glide through by car in the evening or combine trolley and walking. The reward for a cold night is a hot bowl of Texas red chili — the beanless one is the real one.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: The Dallas table rises from two kinds of smoke: oak smoke from the barbecue pit and the sizzle of the fajita skillet — queso on top, a frozen margarita alongside.

local_word.definition: The Tex-Mex form of melted cheese sauce: the sacred opener that reaches the table first, with chips. It's Spanish for 'cheese', but in Texas it's a proper noun — 'do y'all have queso?' is asked before the menu is read. From plain to spiked with meat and peppers, it is every table's opening signature.

items.name: Brisket
items.description: Beef brisket smoked twelve hours over oak: black 'bark' outside, a pink smoke ring within. Cut by the pound at the counter — ask for the moist side and eat it with white bread and pickles. This is the throne of Texas barbecue.
items.tag: The throne · from the moist side

items.name: Tex-Mex and the queso ritual
items.description: It opens with the chips-salsa-queso trio and continues with enchiladas and tacos: Tex-Mex is its own cuisine and Dallas is one of its capitals. The yellow-cheese, ground-beef 'Tex-Mex enchilada' is nostalgia itself.

items.name: The frozen margarita
items.description: The machine-churned margarita was invented in Dallas in 1971: the city's coldest point of pride. Salted rim, ice crystals and Texas heat — the equation was written here; solve it on site.

items.name: Chicken fried steak
items.description: The Texas giant of crisp-battered steak: peppered white gravy on top, mashed potatoes alongside. Found at every level from truck stop to smart brasserie — take the portion warning seriously.

items.name: The breakfast taco morning
items.description: Egg, potato, chorizo and a tortilla: the foldable classic of a Texas morning. Bought at a taquería counter, woken up with salsa verde — taco before coffee is legitimate order here.

items.name: Corny dogs and pecan pie
items.description: Fletcher's fair-born corn dog is the taste of October; pecan pie is the year-round crown of Texas dessert: nutty, caramelly, heavy by the slice. Both are state pride — take them in turn.

callout.label: Table rule
callout.text: In Dallas the barbecue hall is lunch business, not dinner: the good ones close when the meat runs out. In Tex-Mex, choose the family taquería over the tourist window — family photos on the wall and queued locals are the honest signs.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone sees Reunion Tower; these six are Dallas's mural-painted, lake-breezed hidden face.

items.name: White Rock Lake
items.description: A 15-kilometer lakeside loop ten minutes from Downtown: rowers, pelicans and a skyline view. A morning run or bike loop — where Dallasites meet nature.

items.name: The Bishop Arts streets
items.description: Independent shops, empanada bakeries and murals among Oak Cliff's restored bungalows: the city of small scale. The afternoon formula of shop-browsing plus a bakery stop never fails.

items.name: Pioneer Plaza
items.description: In the heart of Downtown, a life-size sculpture herd of 49 bronze steers and three cowboys: among America's largest bronze monuments. Go early — walking alone through the herd is strange and beautiful.

items.name: The walls of Deep Ellum
items.description: Hundreds of murals across forty-odd blocks: with the clubs closed, the streets become a gallery. Walk it on a Sunday morning with coffee — the same neighborhood, an entirely different face by day.

items.name: The Fort Worth Stockyards
items.description: At the Metroplex's far end, a longhorn herd is driven down the street twice a day: stables, rodeo and western outfitters. Touristy yet true — the living stage of Texas mythology.

items.name: Klyde Warren Park
items.description: A park built ON TOP of the freeway that split the city: food trucks, free yoga and a pedestrian bridge to the museum axis. Urban planning's Dallas victory — Saturday noon is its liveliest hour.

callout.label: Two-city strategy
callout.text: Don't mistake the Metroplex for one city: give Dallas the museum-mural-barbecue day and Fort Worth the Stockyards + Kimbell day. The 45-minute road between them is the shortest bridge between two different Texases.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Dallas is an honest city; its traps grow from scale and misplaced expectations — know these four.

items.name: Assuming a walkable city
items.description: Between two points that look close on the map may lie a freeway, mega-blocks and shadeless pavement: Dallas is not a city to 'tour' on foot.
items.instead: Walk within neighborhoods, drive between them: Bishop Arts, Deep Ellum and the Arts District are each walkable inside. On DART-line routes the train is always the smart move.

items.name: Arriving ticketless at the Sixth Floor
items.description: The JFK museum runs timed tickets and sells out on weekends: the walk-up visitor is left with the plaza alone.
items.instead: Buy online days ahead; choose the version with the audio guide. Give no money to the plaza's freelance 'conspiracy guides' — the museum's telling is balanced and sufficient.

items.name: Tourist steakhouse prices
items.description: Some 'Texas steakhouse' windows sell average meat at peak prices with show decor: a waiter in a cowboy hat doesn't change frozen beef.
items.instead: Eat steak at storied local grills and brisket at lunchtime pits: the queue, the oak smoke and the butcher counter are the true signs. A 'sold out' sign is a quality guarantee.

items.name: Expecting the fair without the Fair
items.description: The State Fair runs only from late September to mid-October: other months Fair Park is quiet, some corners neglected — the 'always a festival' expectation ends in disappointment.
items.instead: Outside fair dates, tour Fair Park briefly for its Art Deco architecture and museums; find the festival mood in Bishop Arts weekends and Deep Ellum shows.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: Dallas's formula is hour + queue + neighborhood: early for brisket, ticketed for museums, unhurried for the districts. Say 'howdy' and take your tips from locals — Texas generosity beats any map.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Itineraries
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. Times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

steps.title: Breakfast taco morning
steps.description: Chorizo tacos and coffee from a taquería counter: start the day Texas style.

steps.title: Dealey Plaza and the Sixth Floor Museum
steps.description: Enter with your timed ticket: history stands at the window. Walk the plaza and the X mark with respect.

steps.title: Pioneer Plaza and a Downtown walk
steps.description: Pass through the bronze herd with Reunion Tower behind: the classic frames of the Dallas skyline.

steps.title: Brisket lunch
steps.description: The counter queue at a barbecue hall: moist brisket, ribs and white bread. Go early — the door closes when the meat is gone.

steps.title: Arts District and Klyde Warren
steps.description: Choose the Nasher Sculpture Center or the DMA, then a food-truck coffee break in the park over the highway.

steps.title: Deep Ellum night
steps.description: An evening walk among the murals, a Tex-Mex dinner and a live music club: closing with a frozen margarita.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Museums, cowboys and a lake — the full Metroplex

steps.title: Classic Dallas
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: Dealey Plaza, Pioneer Plaza, brisket, the Arts District, a Deep Ellum night.

steps.title: Neighborhoods and the lake
steps.description: A morning walk at White Rock Lake or the Arboretum; shop-browsing and empanadas in Bishop Arts at noon; the Katy Trail and the M-Line trolley in the afternoon; a porch dinner in Uptown.

steps.title: Fort Worth day
steps.description: The longhorn drive and western outfitters at the Stockyards in the morning; the Kimbell or the Modern at noon; Sundance Square in the afternoon; a farewell Fort Worth steak — two cities, one trip.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Texas English is slow, sweet and full of idiom; these five phrases open doors across the Metroplex.

items.meaning: Hello — Texas's official greeting; comes with a nod
'About to' — when you hear 'I'm fixin' to eat', the table is near
The Texas 'come again' — you'll be sent off with this at the door
For all talk and no substance — use it well and earn applause
The double-verb Southern classic for 'maybe I can' — smile when you hear it; you've understood
